lines.text: This is Hungary's prime minister, Peter Magyar.
On November the fourth, his government opened the communist secret police files to anyone.
About sixty thousand names are now public, Reuters and Euronews report.
Each registration card lists a name, a job, and the grounds for recruitment.
The files sit in Budapest, at the state security archive.
For four decades, the secret police recruited ordinary people to report on others.
The biggest list, about fifty-five thousand names, was kept on magnetic tape.
Magyar had promised this. Earlier governments kept putting it off.
Plus a recruitment register, from nineteen fifty-seven to sixty-two.
But a name on a list is not proof that someone informed.
Many files were lost in nineteen fifty-six, and again as communism fell.
In all, it had about a hundred and fifty thousand agents. Only a third of the names are known.
The archive's director warns the records are very incomplete. Magyar asked for dignity and humanity.
Next: over nine thousand recruitment files, due by February twenty twenty-seven.
